newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli unions take on Netanyahu economic policy.
newsitem.headline: Israeli unions take on Netanyahu economic policy.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu battled an outbreak of nationwide strikes on Sunday in the biggest grassroots challenge to his six-month-old government's programme of budget-slashing and privatisation.

Tens of thousands of workers at seaports and airports, the telephone company, banks, state-owned media and health clinics walked off their jobs during the day in response to a call from Histadrut labour union federation chairman Amir Peretz.

Peretz accelerated the labour action, which began last week, when his trade union section chief, Shlomo Shani, was arrested on Sunday morning by police for failing to appear before a labour court in connection with strikes the Histadrut organised last week.
Netanyahu sought to go over the heads of union leaders and appealed directly to workers not to participate.

"I say to the Histadrut's leaders and dealmakers, the country does not belong to them. It's not their private property that they can use as they wish. It belongs to all the citizens, to all the workers," he told army radio.
Finance Minister Dan Meridor threatened to take unspecified action against the strikers.

Last Thursday the labour federation launched a series of gradually widening strikes that were due to culminate in a general strike on Tuesday, the last day of the year when parliament was due to vote on next year's budget.

The government's 1997 budget proposal calls for seven billion shekels ($2.15 billion) in spending cuts, new taxes and other revenue-raising measures that Netanyahu said were needed to rein in the soaring deficit. The government also promises soon to unveil a wide-ranging privatisation programme and measures designed to increase competition.
Although parliament has forced the Treasury to back down on key parts of the budget, Peretz told army radio it would still hurt working men and women.

Sunday's strikes, which the Histadrut characterised as "spontaneous" and connected only with the arrest, were called off in the evening after Shani's release. But union leaders vowed to continue their labour actions on Monday.
"This is a political, irresponsible and baseless strike," Netanyahu told Israel Radio. "No one understands why the Histadrut went out on this strike."

Peretz is also a member of parliament from the opposition Labour party, but he denied the strike had partisan motives and said that much of the Histadrut's local leadership included activists from Netanyahu's own Likud party.
"The Histadrut only deals in workers' issues opposite every government," Peretz said.
He said the government had been reporting to Histadrut leaders on budgetary measures it planned to take only to change them without notice. "We are talking about the rules of the game," Peretz said.
The Treasury budget package encountered strong opposition among Likud and coalition members of parliament, but powerful grassroots opposition outside parliament never developed.
"I hope (the unions) will take the correct steps to avoid disrupting normal life," Meridor told a news conference.
"If they do not do this, we will take whatever actions are appropriate to enable the normal functioning of society."
